title: Don't insult their gods
hookLine: don't insult what others call on, lest they insult Allah in ignorance (6:108)

cards: Every comment section runs on the same engine. Someone mocks a thing another person loves. The other mocks something back, a little harder.
Within a few replies, both are saying things about each other's most sacred things that neither would say to a face. Nobody's mind has changed; everyone is angrier.
Surah six came in Mecca, when the Muslims were a small group surrounded by people who worshipped idols, and the arguments were real and daily. You might expect the Qur'an to sharpen their tongues.

teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.”
The verb is sabba: to insult, to curse, to abuse with words. Notice what the verse doesn't say.
It doesn't stop disagreeing with idol worship; this same surah argues against it again and again, with stars and seeds and reasons. What it forbids is the insult.

Disagree, explain, argue in the best way, as surah sixteen puts it, with wisdom and good counsel. But don't revile. The reason is practical: insult what they call on, and they may revile Allah in return, out of ignorance.
The verse goes on: to every community We have made their own deeds seem fair to them, and they will return to their Lord, who will tell them what they used to do.
People hold dear what seems fair to them; mock it, and the mockery comes back aimed at what you hold dear. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim works the same way.
The Prophet ﷺ said one of the gravest sins is cursing your own parents. The companions asked, who would curse their own parents?
He said: you insult another man's father, and he insults yours.
Scholars built a principle from texts like these, sadd adh-dhara'i': closing the doors that lead to harm.
Something permitted in itself can become forbidden when it reliably leads somewhere worse. A rude joke about someone else's faith is one of those doors.

how: Muslim scholars cite 6:108 to forbid mocking what others hold sacred, and use it as a classic example of sadd adh-dhara'i', blocking the means to harm; some imams quote it in interfaith settings.

o: to insult or revile with words
to stay silent about your own faith
to argue firmly against a belief

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: argue with wisdom and good counsel

s: 6:108 means Muslims may not disagree with other beliefs
the surah argues against idol worship often. it forbids insult, not disagreement.
the verse was revealed when Muslims were a small group in Mecca
a hadith says insulting another's father is a way of cursing your own
he insults yours in return (Bukhari and Muslim).

games.q: you're with friends, and someone starts mocking a neighbor's religion. what does 6:108's logic suggest?
o: join in. it's only a joke.
don't join the insult; disagree, if you must, with respect.
mock theirs back to balance it.
games.why: revile not, lest they revile Allah in ignorance. the verse forbids insult and leaves room for respectful disagreement.

practice: Bring to mind a faith or practice that isn't yours, one you've joked about or heard joked about, and picture a real person who holds it dear, a grandmother, a classmate, a neighbor, and their face when it's mocked.
Then find one respectful sentence you could say about their faith, something true, said the way you'd want yours spoken of, and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Sabba, to insult, to revile with words. Surah six, verse one-oh-eight: revile not what others call on, or they'll revile Allah in ignorance. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: and do not insult (6:108), from sabba, to revile.

carryVoice: Your line: don't insult. Disagreement can stay; the insult goes. That's day four hundred three.

sources.q: Revile not those unto whom they pray beside Allah lest they wrongfully revile Allah through ignorance.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5973; Sahih Muslim 90 (cursing one's parents)
